newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-OPINION-Migrants scapegoats for Australian unemployment.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-OPINION-Migrants scapegoats for Australian unemployment.

text.p: The controversy generated by a number of parliamentarians surrounding immigration to Australia has been decidedly lacking in statistics and substance.
There is a need to clarify a number of issues to enable better informed discussion.
Countrary to general misconceptions, the level of immigration to Australia is low.
Australia's non-humanitarian migration program for 1996/97 is planned at 74,000 compared with an outcome of 82,500 for the previous financial year.
In a nation with a population of less than one new resident per two hundred existing residents.
Popular opinion on the level of immigration is flawed.
In addition to the non-humanitarian programme Australia also has a Humanitarian Immigration Programme which plans to see some 12,000 migrants arrive in 1996/97.
This is less than the previous year's outcome of 15,052.
Some would argue that this category of immigration should also be subject to further reduction.
However, Australia has international humanitarian obligations which include accepting refugees from the world's various trouble spots.

Net overseas migration in 1994/95 of 83,600 (or about 0.5 percent of the total population) and significantly lower than the high in net migration of 149,500 or 1.8 percent of the total population in 1949/50.
Between 1950 and 1970 net migration was generally running at about one percent of the total population or roughly double current rates.
AUSTRALIA NOT OVERRUN WITH NEW IMMIGRANTS

It is doubtful most Australians, especially those responding to questions from pollsters, have the vaguest idea on what the current level of immigration to Australia is in the first place. Australia is not being over run with new immigrants.
There is some concern that migrants from Asia dominate the immigrant intake to Australia. This is also incorrect.
Migrants from Southeast and Northeast Asia amounted to 24,760 in 1994-95 which is less than one third of permanent settler arrivals for that period.
Migrants from Europe represented the largest geographical source of migrants.

On a country basis, the UK and NZ are the largest sources of new migrants around 10,500 each in 1994-95 (representing one quarter of the permanent settler arrivals) followed by Viet Nam and the Philippines with 5,097 and 4,116 respectively.
Furthermore, the 1991 census shows that 577,700 or 3.2 percent of the total population were born in Southeast and Northeast Asia.
These figures are also contrary to assertions by some commentators that Australia is undergoing some sort of "Asianisation".
The Coalition Government is placing more emphasis on increasing the number of migrants arriving in Australia with special skills.
STRONG CASE FOR BOOSTING INTAKE OF SKILLED MIGRANTS
This is being done at the expense of the family based intake. On economic criteria there is a strong case in favour of boosting the intake of skilled migrants.
The planned intake of skilled migrants for 1996/97 is 28,000 compared with an outcome of 24,100 for 1995/96.
Skilled migrants benefit the economy by meeting skills shortages as well as constraining wage growth and hence alleviating wage driven inflationary pressure.

Skilled migrants represent the cost effective importation of skilled labour. Cost effective, for the simple reason that Australia has not devoted resources on the education and training of these skilled immigrants.
Australis is in effect taking the human capital of those nations which have invested in training and education of these skilled individuals and putting that human capital to work here.
On economic grounds it can be advocated that this category be further increased at the expense of the family based intake.
The difficulty is that it is unrealistic to expect migrants not to eventually assist other close family members to come to Australia as well.
There are social costs associated with existing migrants not being able to unite with close family members.
UNEMPLOYMENT A DEEP SEATED PROBLEM
There appears to be some hostility towards immigration on the grounds that migrants are taking the jobs of Australians.

Blaming the nation's 800,200 unemployed upon a net migrant intake of less than 100,000 has overtones of migrants being used as scapegoats for more deep seated problems which have resulted in Australia enduring a high unemployment rate.
From an economic point of view, migrants generate more demand for goods and services which in turn create more employment opportunities than the number of jobs which new migrants would fill.
In net terms employment prospects are increased.
Population growth is a fundamental source of economic growth which often translates into more employment opportunities.

The nation's high unemployment rate is more related to a lack of flexibility in industrial relations, a lack of employment orientated training and education, insufficient business investment, a small business sector over laden with regulatins, and the need for the nation to be more export orientated .... just to name a few issues.

Highlighting the benefits of immigration, as well as the factors which have left Australia with so many unemployed would go some way to reducing the aversion, some would even say hostility, towards further migration to Australia.
ENVIRONMENT ARGUMENT MISCHIEVOUS

The unemployment argument is analoguous to arguments made by environmentalists against immigration - namely that the boost to population from migrants will place additional pressure on the local environment. This is a mischievous argument.

If governments were committed to environmental protection then it would be in the interests of the environment to focus on the activities of all 18 million people and not the marginal effect that additional migrants will have onthe nation.

Pollution could be curtailed and the environment better protected by encourageing 18 million Australians to use public transport, invest in better insulation for their homes and government pricing policies on water, for example, that reflect the relative scarcity of water.
The implementation of these sorts of policies would have a more beneficial effect on the environment than the marginal environmental degradation which could be attributed to new immigrants.
There is more at stake than a small number of misguided parliamentarians expressing their opposition to immigration in generla, and Asian immigration in particular.
DEBATE BEING HIJACKED
The immigration debate is being hijacked by populist perceptions that immigration is too high, Australia is undergoing an "Asianisation" and that immigration directly leadst to higher unemployment.

In addition, these misguided views not only detract the public's attention from what needs to be done to reduce unemployment, such as a more flexible industrial relations environment, but are also sowing the seeds of racial hositility for many years to come.
Numerous polls have been conducted on what more established Australian citizens think about the level of immigration to Australia.
It would be more instructive, however, if a poll was commissioned to interivew recent migrants, say from Asia, on how they were made to feel and what they thought of more established Australians.

The nation's political leaders, as well as notable opinion makers, preferred to take the politically unpalatable course of highlighting the key factors driving our high unemployment rate, then Pauline Hanson, as well as those who are like-minded, would have less populist appeal.
What is disappointing is the absence of parliamentarians prepared to raise some of the economic arguments outlined above ore even use hard statistics on immigration.
RELIANCE ON INNOCUOUS AND SIMPLE VIEW
Instead, there has been a reliance on the innocuous and simple view that opinions expressed by parliamentarians such as Pauline Hanson will damage trade with Asia.

Either the nation's parliamentarians are not familiar with statistical sources or our parliamentarians are not prepared to challenge what the perceive to be populist viws which have electoral support.

It is inevitable to ask why there appears to be such support for anti-immigration/anti-Asian views inthe first place, particularly given the contribution made by migrants to this country since the Second World War.
According to a "Newspoll" published in "The Australain" on 4 October 1996 some 80 percent of respondents with incomes less than A$30,000 thought that immigration was "too high".
This compares with 58 percent of respondents with incomes in excess of A$50,000 who thought that immigration was "too high".
Therein is a possible explanation.

It is possible those with low incomes feel economically threatened and also see recent migrants and the children of recent migrants achieve economic and social prosperity greater than they or their children are likely to obtain.
Rectifying such feelings of insecurity and envy are not readily achieved by economic policy and are always likely to be manipulated by ill informed parliamentarians and populist commentators.
-- Sydney Newsroom 61-2 373-1800
